chapters.title: Welcome to Docket
chapters.html:
Docket is the task manager for everyone at Legend of Toys. Whatever the work is, marketing, production, finance, a one-off errand, it becomes a task with a clear owner and a deadline, and you can follow it from the moment it is captured to the moment it is done. This manual is your self-serve guide to every screen in it.

What Docket is for

Docket answers three questions for the whole company at once: what needs doing, who is accountable for it, and is it on track. It is deliberately simple to use, type a title and press Enter and you have captured a task, and just as deliberately honest about the past: once a deadline is set it cannot be quietly edited away, and a task can never be silently deleted.

The shape of a task

Every task carries the same handful of things. You will see them again and again throughout the app.

On a taskWhat it means
OwnerThe one person accountable for getting it done. A task has exactly one owner.
CollaboratorsOther people helping. They can comment and add notes and sub-tasks, but the owner stays accountable.
TeamThe department the task belongs to, drawn live from the company's people directory.
StatusOne of five: Not started, In progress, Done, Blocked, or Abandoned.
PriorityP0 (immediate) through P3 (low). P2 is the normal default.
DeadlineWhen it is due. The first deadline you set is locked as the original promise; later changes are recorded as revisions.
PlanAn optional link to the goal (a theme, milestone or result) the task serves. Tasks with no link are called Unplanned.
IDA permanent number like DKT-1042 that never changes, so a task can always be found and quoted.
ⓘ Two principles to remember

Docket keeps an honest record. The original deadline is locked the first time it is set, every later change is logged with a reason, so “when did we promise this?” always has an answer. And tasks are never deleted; a task you decide not to do is Abandoned (with a reason), which keeps it on the record rather than erasing it.

How the work is organised

Docket organises work in two different ways, and they answer different questions:

  • A Space decides who can see a task. It is a private, walled-off area; only its members can see the tasks inside it, even admins are shut out unless invited. Everything that is not in a private space lives in the open General space.
  • The Plan decides why the work matters. It is the company’s list of goals (themes, milestones and results), and a task can be linked to one so that the weekly review can show how much of the week’s work moved a goal. It changes nothing about who can see a task. The old Programs label has been retired in its favour.

On top of that, Docket counts the week as a unit: every deadline falls in a “week ending”, each team gets an on-time score for the week, and a weekly review pulls it together. Those ideas have their own part of this manual, The Plan.

How to use this manual

Each chapter covers one screen or one idea and follows the same shape: what it is for, how to read it, and what to do. Jump to the screen you are on using the Contents page or your PDF reader's bookmarks. Chapters are tagged with the roles that use them:

Member   Reviewer   Admin   Founder   Associate

Member, Reviewer and Admin cover the task manager. Founder and Associate describe extra access to the Plan and the review; see Roles & What You Can See.

Callout boxes

✓ Tip

A faster or smarter way to do something.

⚠ Watch out

A common mistake or something easy to misread.

⛔ Important

Something permanent or audited: get it right the first time.

chapters.title: Signing In & Getting Around
chapters.html:
Docket opens with one click using your work Google account. Once you are in, a slim icon rail on the left takes you between the main screens, a sidebar beside it holds the Plan and your Spaces, and a top bar carries search and the + New button. This chapter covers signing in and finding your way around, on a computer and on a phone.

Signing in

Open docket.legendoftoys.com and press Sign in with Google on the sign-in card, using your @legendoftoys.com account. Personal accounts are refused; if sign-in bounces you back, sign out of any personal Google account first or use a fresh browser profile. There is nothing to set up, your account already knows which team you are on and what you are allowed to see.

The icon rail (computer)

The narrow strip at the far left is the main menu. Each icon has its name under it, and the page you are on is highlighted in yellow. You only ever see the icons your role allows.

IconWhere it goes
PlanThe company plan: the register for Founders, My milestones for everyone else. See Themes, Milestones & Results.
TasksThe Tasks list for the open General space (and any space you pick in the sidebar).
My tasksEverything on your plate across every space you can see.
ChecklistYour recurring work.
ScratchpadYour private notes and calculator.
DashboardThe org-wide review screen. Only appears if you have been given it.
ManualThis manual.
AdminRoles & permissions, Users and Spaces. Sits at the bottom of the rail, admins only.

At the very bottom of the rail is your avatar (your initial in a coloured circle). Click it for your name and role, Keyboard shortcuts and Sign out.

The sidebar: Plan and Spaces

Next to the rail, on the Tasks and Plan screens, the sidebar holds the Plan and your Spaces. Programs no longer have a sidebar section; the Plan has taken their place, and old program links still open as a read-only list.

Plan

At the top, a Plan row, then a short list beneath it. Which rows you see depends on who you are:

  • Three weeks, Tree and Review: everyone.
  • Templates: only if you may make or use a template.
  • Re-plan and Founders’ catch-up: Founders only.

Each has its own chapter in The Plan part.

Spaces

General (the open space, always there), then My spaces (private spaces you own) and By others (private spaces someone added you to). The + beside the heading creates a new space.

Each group has a small arrow to fold it open or shut, and Docket remembers your choice. Customize sidebar at the bottom lets you tick whether to show My spaces and By others. The sidebar can be hidden to give the list more room: use the panel button at the left of the top bar, or press [.

On an Admin screen the sidebar switches to the three admin pages instead (see the Administration part).

The top bar

PartWhat it does
BreadcrumbWhere you are, for example the space name. A padlock marks a private space. A number beside it shows how many tasks are on the screen.
Search boxReads Search tasks… with ⌘K beside it (Ctrl K on Windows). Click it to open the command bar (below), which finds tasks in every space you can open.
+ NewThe yellow button. The main part starts a new task. The small arrow beside it offers New task and New space.
?Opens the keyboard-shortcuts sheet.
App launcherJumps to the other Legend of Toys apps.

The command bar: search and jump

Press ⌘K (Ctrl K on Windows and Linux), or click the search box, to open the command bar from any screen. Type a few letters and it fuzzy-matches across:

  • Tasks, in every space you can open: by title or DKT- number. Type at least two characters, or a number in any form (247, DKT-247 or #247). Words match in any order, so sop qc finds a task called “QC checks for SOP”. If nothing matches exactly, Docket tries a typo-tolerant match (chekclist finds Checklist); that fallback appears only when there are no exact hits. Each result shows its space and, for a sub-task, its parent (↳ DKT-…) on a desktop screen. Enter opens the task in place; Ctrl/⌘ + Enter opens it as a full page.
  • Spaces: jump straight to one.
  • Navigation: any screen you can reach from the rail.
  • Commands: New task / space, Go to My tasks, switch List or Board view and row density (on the Tasks list), toggle the sidebar, keyboard shortcuts. While a task you can edit is open, Add dependency to DKT-… also appears (see Inside a Task).

With nothing typed it shows your last five picks under Recent, kept separately for each person on a shared browser. Use ↑ ↓ to move, Enter to run, Esc to close. While it looks across spaces the bar shows Searching all spaces….

ⓘ You only find what you could open

Search follows the same rule as opening a task. In General you find tasks that are yours, in your department, or that you collaborate on (everyone with view-all finds every General task). A private space’s tasks appear only if you own it or are a member of it, and that includes admins. It works from any screen, not just the Tasks list.

Where you land

When you open Docket it sends you to the right place for your role. Founders and reviewers, the people who can see everything, land on the Dashboard. Everyone else lands on the Tasks list, which is where day-to-day work happens.

Keyboard shortcuts

  • ⌘K / Ctrl K opens the command bar from anywhere, even while typing.
  • / jumps into the search box on the Tasks list; on every other screen it opens the command bar.
  • c starts a new task, and [ (or ⌘\) hides or shows the sidebar.
  • ? shows the full shortcut sheet.
  • The Tasks list and an open task have their own keys, covered in those chapters.

On a phone

At phone width (767 pixels and narrower) the rail and sidebar give way to a tab bar along the bottom:

Tabs

Tasks, My tasks, Checklist, then Dashboard if you have it (otherwise Scratchpad), and More.

More

Plan, Scratchpad (when Dashboard has taken its tab), Manual, Admin for admins, Keyboard shortcuts and Sign out.

Plan and Spaces

Tap the menu button at the left of the top bar to slide the sidebar in. The top bar also has search and a + that starts a new task.

The Manual (this guide) opens inside the same frame. On a phone it shows a Contents button to pick a chapter and a PDF button to download the printable version.

✓ Quick capture on the go

The yellow + in the top bar is always one tap away on a phone. Type the title, add it, and tidy up later.

chapters.title: Roles & What You Can See
chapters.html:
Docket gives each person the access that matches their job. Unlike some systems, having no special role in Docket is not the same as having no access, every signed-in LOT person is a full Member. This chapter explains the roles used throughout this manual and what each unlocks: three for the task manager, and two more for the company Plan.

The three task-manager roles

Member

Everyone, by default. Any signed-in LOT person is a Member without an admin doing anything. A Member creates tasks, and sees their own tasks, anything they are a collaborator on, and every task in their own department. They can fully edit the tasks they own or created (and add comments, documents and sub-tasks to any task they can see).

Reviewer

The watcher. A Reviewer sees every task across the whole company, plus the review Dashboard, but read-only. They can look at anything but do not change other people's tasks. Useful for managers and leads who need the full picture.

Admin

Full control. An Admin can see and edit any task, decide who has which role, share the Dashboard, and use the admin screens. Admin includes everything a Reviewer can do.

Two more roles, for the Plan

The Plan (themes, milestones, targets and the weekly review) has its own, narrower access. Two further roles exist for it. Both are given only by a Founder, and most people have neither.

Founder

The super admin. A Founder sees the whole Plan, including each item’s target and the founders-only themes; agrees, re-dates, splits, drops and finishes milestones; decides proposals; sets the Founders’ top 5; and uses the Re-plan and Founders’ catch-up screens. A Founder is also an Admin, and can see every team’s review and score. Only a Founder can give this role to anyone, change it, or remove it.

Associate

The Founders’ Associate. Reads every plan item that is not founders-only, in full except the targets, and the weekly review for any team. It is read-only: an Associate does not change the Plan, and does not see the Founders’ catch-up or re-plan. It is a separate role from Reviewer and Admin and does not include either. Also given only by a Founder.

Everyone else, whatever their task role, sees the Plan through the lens in the next table: the titles of themes that are not founders-only, plus the milestones and results they own.

In the PlanEveryoneAssociateFounder
Titles of themes that are not founders-only•••
The milestones and results you own, and propose new ones•••
Every milestone and result that is not founders-only••
The weekly review for any teamown team••
Targets, founders-only themes, the Founders’ space•
Edit the Plan, decide proposals, Re-plan, Founders’ catch-up•

The full picture is in Themes, Milestones & Results, under Who sees what in the Plan.

ⓘ How access actually works

Your access comes from a role an admin assigns you on the Users page. Most people have no role, which is the Member baseline above. Two switches sit behind the scenes: one lets a person see all org tasks and the Dashboard (that is the Reviewer), the other adds full management on top (that is the Admin). Two more switches, under Plan on the Roles screen, give the Founder and Associate access to the Plan. The tags in this manual are plain-language names for those switches. If you cannot do something you think you should, an admin needs to adjust your role.

Who sees what

AreaMemberReviewerAdmin
Create tasks; use the Scratchpad•••
See own + collaborator + own-team tasks•••
Edit the tasks you own or created•••
See every task in the company (read-only)••
The review Dashboardif shared••
Edit / abandon any task•
Link your tasks to the Plan, propose, hand a task to another team•••
Roles, Users, Spaces, dashboard sharing•
✓ Seeing a task is not the same as editing it

A Reviewer can open every task but the controls are simply not there for them, they read. Collaborators are in between: they can comment, attach documents and add sub-tasks on a task, but the core fields (owner, deadline, status) stay in the hands of the owner, the creator, or an admin.

Two things that sit outside roles

Two parts of Docket are governed separately from the three roles above, and both get their own chapters:

  • The Dashboard can be handed to anyone, even a plain Member, without making them a Reviewer. See The Dashboard.
  • Private Spaces are gated by membership, not role. Being an Admin does not let you into someone's private space; you have to be added (or break in through the audited admin recovery). See Spaces.

parts.subtitle: Capturing work, the task list, the task view, and how a task lives from first idea to done.

chapters.title: The Tasks List
chapters.html:
The Tasks list is where you live. It is one screen that captures new work, shows what is on your plate, and lets you edit almost everything in the row without opening anything. Tasks are laid out as a tidy list of rows, grouped under collapsible headers, with columns you can show, hide and resize. This chapter is the longest in the manual because it covers the screen you will use most.

What it’s for
Capturing, finding, and updating tasks.
Read or act?
Both: read your list and edit in place.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Shows
The tasks you’re allowed to see, in one space (or across spaces on My tasks).

The layout

From top to bottom the screen has:

Views bar

A List / Board switch, a greyed-out + View (saved views are coming later), and on the right a Copy link button. In a private space it also has a space dashboard button, and, for the space’s owner, a space settings button.

Toolbar

On the left, Group and Subtasks. On the right, Filter, Me, Archive done, Select, the search box, Columns, Customize and the yellow + Task button. On a phone the labelled buttons shrink to icons.

The list

The column header row, then the groups of tasks, each with its own header and a + Add task line at the foot.

Capturing a task in one line

Click + Task (or press c, or use + New in the top bar) and a New task line opens under the toolbar. Type a title, press Enter, and the task exists. That is the whole capture step, no form, no required fields. The new task lands in The Grid so you can finish it off later.

Quick-add: type it, don’t click it

The capture line (the top + Task line, each group’s + Add task line, and a Board column’s add line) reads a few shortcuts out of the title and turns them into Owner, Deadline and Priority chips before you save, so you can check what Docket understood.

TypeYou get
@riyaOwner. A first name, or a prefix that matches only one person. If two people fit, it stays as plain text.
!p0 to !p3Priority P0 to P3.
today, tomorrow / tmrwThat day.
by fri, fri 5pm, or a weekday as the last wordThe next such weekday. A weekday in the middle of a sentence (“Sat with Riya”) stays text.
12 nov, nov 12, 12/11A date; slash dates are day/month. 12/11 counts only if it is a future date within 60 days, so “3/4 sleeve” stays text.
5pm, 5:30pm, 17:00A time (Indian time). A date with no time means 6 pm.

The words that became a chip leave the title. Docket never sets a deadline in the past: a time that has already passed today rolls to tomorrow, and a date that cannot be read as a future one stays in the title. Pick a value from a chip yourself and it wins over the typed words, which go back into the title. Click the × on a chip to drop it and keep the words as text.

You can also capture straight into a group: every group ends with a + Add task line, and the task is created already carrying that group’s value (grouped by Owner, a new task gets that owner; grouped by Team, that team; grouped by Status, a task added under In progress is created in that status straight away). The group header has an Add task button too, which jumps you to that line. With a row focused, c opens its own group’s line.

✓ Capture first, tidy later

Do not stop to fill in the owner and deadline while an idea is fresh. Get the title down, hit Enter, and move on. The Grid will remind you what still needs finishing.

The Grid: tasks that need setting up

Just-captured tasks sit in a dashed yellow group at the top of the list called The Grid, with the hint needs an owner and a deadline to hit the board. A task is in the Grid whenever it is missing an owner or a deadline (or both). Each Grid card has two small chips, Owner and Deadline: click one to fill it in right there. The moment a task has both, it leaves the Grid on its own and joins the main list below. Click the Grid’s header to fold it away.

Triage The Grid

When the Grid has tasks you can edit, its header shows a Triage N button. It walks you through them one at a time, so a backlog of half-finished tasks takes minutes instead of a lot of clicking. Each card shows the task and the fields still needed; set the Owner and Deadline (you can type something like fri 5pm into the deadline box) and a progress line at the top tracks how far you are.

KeyWhat it does
EnterSave & next.
AAbandon the task. A reason is required and logged.
SSkip it and leave it in the Grid.
←Back to the previous card.
EscClose. The list refreshes when you close.

Only the fields you actually touched are saved, and a deadline in the past is refused. A task that has both an owner and a deadline after saving leaves the Grid; one that still lacks one stays. Tasks you cannot edit are skipped.

Reading a row

Each task is one row, 36 pixels tall by default. At the left is a round tick circle (click it to mark the task done, or not done), then the title. The columns to the right are:

ColumnWhat it shows
NameThe title, with the permanent DKT- number beside it (turn the numbers off in Customize). A REV tag means the deadline has been changed at least once. A sub-task count like 2/5 shows done out of total.
StatusNot started / In progress / Done / Blocked / Abandoned. Always shown.
TeamThe department it belongs to.
PlanThe plan item the task is linked to, shown as its code (hover for the title). An empty cell offers Set plan. See Linking Tasks to the Plan.
SpaceWhich space it lives in. Appears only on My tasks, which spans several spaces.
OwnerThe accountable person, as an initial circle (hover for the full name).
CollaboratorsHelpers, as small overlapping initial circles. Hover to see names.
PriorityA flag for P0 (immediate) to P3 (low).
DeadlineWhen it is due. Turns red once the date has passed on an open task.
ActivitySmall counts of attached documents and comments.

The dependency icon

A task that is part of a dependency shows a small icon beside its title, on list rows and on board cards:

  • Red “waiting” icon with a number: the task is waiting on that many open tasks.
  • “Blocking” icon with a number: that many open tasks are waiting for this one.
  • Grey tick: the task had blockers and every one is now cleared (done or abandoned).

Hover for a one-line summary. Click to open a small popover listing the linked tasks: click one to open it, or use the x to remove a link if you can edit the task. Open DKT-… to add links at the bottom takes you into the task, where new links are added (see Inside a Task). Tasks with no links show no icon. Marking a waiting task done asks for confirmation first, from the tick circle, the board and bulk updates alike.

Shaping the columns

  • Show or hide: the Columns button lists every optional column with a tick. Name and Status are always on. Reset columns puts everything back to the defaults.
  • Resize: drag the thin edge on the right of a column header.
  • Reorder: drag a column header onto another one.
  • Sort: click a header (Name, Status, Owner, Priority, Deadline). Click again to reverse, and a third time to switch sorting off.

Docket remembers your column choices on this device.

Customize: row density and ID numbers

The Customize button (the sliders icon) sets how roomy the list is: Compact (32 pixel rows), Default (36) or Roomy (44). Under Show it also toggles the DKT- ids and the Team column. On the Board, Customize sets card size instead (below).

Editing without opening anything

This is the heart of the screen. If you are allowed to edit a task, most cells are click-to-edit right in the row:

  1. Click a property cell (Status, Team, Plan, Owner or Priority) and a small picker opens, with a search box for the long lists. Pick a value and it saves instantly. An empty cell shows a faint icon when you hover it.
  2. Click the Deadline cell to open a calendar. The first time, you just pick a date. After that, changing it asks for a reason (see below).
  3. Click the Collaborators cell’s small + to add a helper from a short list.
  4. Click the row itself (the title or empty space) to open the task. See Inside a Task.
  5. Use the row’s buttons. Hover a row to reveal + (add a sub-task) and … (Open, Copy link, Add sub-task, Mark done, Abandon).
⚠ Revising a deadline always needs a reason

The first deadline you put on a task is its locked original promise, set with no questions asked. Every change after that asks for a short reason and is recorded on the task’s history. This is on purpose: it is how Docket can always answer “why did this slip?”. See The Task Lifecycle for the full story.

ⓘ If a row won’t let you edit

You can only change the core fields of tasks you own or created (admins can change any). On tasks you merely collaborate on or can only view, the cells simply will not turn into editors. Abandoned tasks are read-only too. That is expected, not a glitch.

Keyboard on the list

Click a row to focus it (or Tab to it), then:

  • ↓ ↑ (or j k) move between rows, and Enter opens the task.
  • x (or Space) toggles done.
  • → / ← (or l / h) expand or collapse its sub-tasks, and s adds a sub-task.
  • f opens Filter and g opens the Group menu.

Sub-tasks

A task can hold a list of sub-tasks (one level deep, sub-tasks cannot themselves have sub-tasks). When a task has them, an arrow and a done/total count appear next to its title; click the arrow to open the children as indented rows underneath. To add one, hover the parent row and click + (or press s); type a title and press Enter. New sub-tasks inherit the parent’s team and owner, which you can change afterwards.

The Subtasks button in the toolbar has Expand all and Collapse all, and a choice between showing sub-tasks Nested under parent (the default) or As separate tasks, where every sub-task gets a row of its own. It appears once at least one task has sub-tasks.

Groups

The Group button on the left of the toolbar regroups the list by Owner, Team, Status or Week ending (or No grouping). Week ending gives one group per week, with Overdue first and No date last; see Weeks and Week Ending. Each group has a header with its name and a count. Click the header to collapse or expand the group; its … menu also offers Collapse all groups and Expand all groups. Docket remembers which groups you folded. An x on the Group button clears the grouping.

Finding tasks: search and filter

Search

The box on the right of the toolbar (press / to jump in) filters as you type, instantly. It matches the ID, title, owner, team, creator and collaborator names, and every word you type must match somewhere. For a search across spaces and screens use the command bar (⌘K).

Filter

Opens a small panel to filter by Status, Team, Owner, Priority, Plan (a theme, milestone or result, or Unplanned) and Week (This week, Next week, Week ending…, Overdue, No date), with quick Overdue and Revised toggles, and a Dependencies pair: Waiting on others (tasks still waiting on an open blocker) and Blocking others (tasks others are still waiting on). Only one of the two can be on at a time, and a blocker that is already done or abandoned does not count. A number on the button says how many filters are on; Clear filters resets them.

Me

A one-click toggle that limits the list to tasks you own, are assigned, collaborate on or raised.

Archive done

Moves finished tasks out of the main list into a collapsed Archived section at the bottom, so the list shows only live work. Untick a task there to bring it back.

List view and Board view

The List / Board switch in the views bar flips between the two, and Docket remembers your choice. (My tasks is list-only.)

List view

The default: tasks as rows, with The Grid, inline editing, sub-tasks and bulk select, all as described above.

Board view

A Kanban: tasks become cards in columns. By default the columns are the statuses (Not started, In progress, Blocked, Done). Use Group to switch the columns to Owner, Team or Week ending instead. The week columns are read-only: a card cannot be dragged to another week, because a deadline only moves by revising it with a reason.

To move a task, drag its card into another column. On a status board, dragging a card to Done marks it done; on an Owner board it reassigns the owner, and so on. Only cards you are allowed to edit move. From the keyboard, focus a card and press Shift + ← / → to move it one column; plain arrows walk between cards, and Enter opens the task.

  • Collapse a column: use the column’s … menu, then Collapse column. It folds to a thin strip with the card count; click the strip to bring it back.
  • Add a card: each column has its own add line, and the new task is created with that column’s value.
  • Card size: Customize offers Small, Medium and Large cards, and a toggle for the DKT- ids.
ⓘ What the board shows

Each card shows the title, DKT- number, owner, priority, deadline and any team, plan or space tags and a hand-off chip, plus small sub-task, comment and document counts. Only top-level tasks appear as cards (a parent shows its sub-task count rather than separate cards), and Abandoned tasks are left off the board. Columns, Archive done, Select and row density are list-only tools.

Plan, week and hand-off on the list

Three ideas from The Plan part show up on every list:

  • Plan. The Plan column and the Plan chip on board cards show the goal a task is linked to; the Plan filter narrows to a theme, milestone, result or Unplanned. On the capture line, a Plan chip sits beside Owner, Deadline and Priority once there is something to link to. Only top-level tasks carry a link; sub-tasks inherit their parent’s.
  • Week. Group › Week ending and the Week filter work on the List, the Grid and the Board.
  • Hand-off. A task given to another team shows a small chip such as → Design on its row, grid card and board card, amber until it is accepted. The same task appears in the receiving team’s Incoming section on My tasks.

Updating many tasks at once

When you need to make the same change to several tasks (assign them all to one person, push them all to next week, bump them all to P1), use bulk update instead of editing each row by hand. It works in The Grid and in the main list.

  1. Click Select in the toolbar (or tick any row’s box). A tick box appears on the left of every task you are allowed to edit. Tasks you only collaborate on or can view show a faint, locked box: you cannot pick those.
  2. Tick the tasks you want. Pick them one by one, or use Select all to grab every editable task currently shown (your search and filters decide what “all” means).
  3. Use the bar that pops up at the bottom. It shows how many are selected and has one button each for Owner, Status, Priority, Deadline, Collaborators (add or remove), Move (to another space) and Abandon.
  4. Pick a value and it applies to every selected task at once. The x at the left of the bar clears the selection; clicking Select again leaves bulk mode.
ⓘ Only your tasks change

A bulk action only touches tasks you are allowed to edit, which is why collaborator-only tasks cannot be ticked in the first place. If a few in your selection still cannot be changed, Docket updates the rest and tells you how many it skipped.

⚠ Bulk deadlines still keep the audit trail

Setting a deadline in bulk follows the same rule as a single task: tasks getting their first deadline are set silently, but if any selected task already has one, Docket asks for a single reason and records the change on each task’s history. Abandoning in bulk likewise needs one reason.

Which space am I in?

The list shows one space at a time. By default that is General, the open company-wide space. If you click a private space in the sidebar, the breadcrumb shows its name (with a padlock) and the list shows only that space’s tasks; anything you capture lands in that space. Spaces have their own chapter. (Programs, which used to gather tasks from every space, are retired. An old program link still opens a read-only list of its tasks with a note pointing to the Plan.)

My tasks: everything on your plate, across every space

My tasks on the rail is different from the rest of the list. Instead of one space, it pulls together every task you are involved in across all the spaces you can see, in four groups (empty groups are hidden):

Today & overdue

Open tasks you own whose deadline is today or earlier, with the most overdue first. “Today” runs to the end of the day in Indian time, and the group re-sorts itself if you leave the tab open past midnight.

Assigned to me

The rest of the tasks you own. Its + Add task line creates a task already assigned to you.

Collaborating

Tasks where you are a collaborator but not the owner.

Raised by me

Open tasks you created that someone else owns, so you can keep an eye on what you handed off.

When another team has handed a task to you or your team, an Incoming section appears above these groups, with To you and To your team tabs and an Accept button on each. It is hidden when nothing is incoming. See Hand-offs.

Because it spans spaces, each row carries a Space column so you can see where a task lives. Every task is its own row here (no nesting of sub-tasks). Search, filters and bulk select work as on a normal list.

Clean up: the stale-work sweep

The Clean up N button at the top of My tasks opens /tasks?lens=stale, a list of your open work (sub-tasks included, recurring tasks not) that is overdue by 30 days or more or untouched for 60 days or more. Each row says why: 145d over or untouched 154d. A task that is both appears once, under Overdue.

Done

Marks the task done.

Revise

Pick a new deadline and give a reason (logged). A past date is refused. If the task never had a deadline the button reads Set date and no reason is asked.

Abandon

Stops the task; a reason is required.

Tick several rows for a bulk Done all or Abandon all (one reason for all). On a phone the row actions sit in a … menu. People with view-all (Reviewers and admins) get a Mine | Everyone switch; Everyone groups the list by owner with an owner filter, but covers only spaces you can access (private spaces need membership). The sweep is pull-only: nothing is sent to anyone.

⚒ A typical pass through your list

Open My tasks and clear Today & overdue first. Then glance at The Grid on the Tasks list and set an owner and deadline on anything sitting there. Sort by Deadline to bring the soonest to the top, and clear anything shown in red. Click a task to open it when you need comments or sub-tasks. Once in a while, use Clean up to retire or re-date work that has gone stale.

chapters.title: Inside a Task
chapters.html:
Click a task anywhere in Docket and it opens in the task view: everything about that one task in a single place. By default it opens as a modal, a window over your list, and you can switch it to a side panel or a full page whenever you prefer. All three show the same task.

What it’s for
Working on one task in depth.
How to open
Click a task row, card or Grid item.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Three layouts
Modal (default), side panel, full page.

Modal, side panel, full page

Modal

The default. A centred window over a dimmed list. Click the dimmed area or press Esc to close it.

Side panel

A panel on the right while the list stays visible, scrollable and clickable behind it. Good for working down a list.

Full page

The task takes the whole screen inside Docket’s normal frame. The top-right button then reads Back to the list and returns you to the list with the task still open.

Switch with the Switch layout button in the task’s top bar (Open tasks as Modal, Side panel or Full page). Docket remembers your choice on this device. On a phone the task always fills the screen, with Details and Activity tabs at the top.

The top bar of the task

PartWhat it does
‹ › arrowsStep to the previous or next task in the list you opened it from, without closing (Ctrl Shift ← / →). They grey out at either end.
BreadcrumbThe space and the DKT- number. Click the number to copy it.
Copy linkCopies a link that opens straight to this task as a full page.
More actions (…)Copy link, Copy task id, Add sub-task, Mark done, and Abandon…. On an abandoned task it offers Reactivate.
Switch layoutModal / Side panel / Full page.
Close (x)Closes the task. Also Esc.

What’s on the task

The left side holds the task itself; the right side (or the Activity tab on a phone) holds the conversation.

SectionWhat it holds
Title and descriptionThe title (and, on a sub-task, a link up to its parent) and a free-text description. If you can edit the task, click either to change it.
Properties panelA tidy list of fields: Status, Owner, Collaborators, Deadline, Priority, Team, Plan, Hand-off to, Space, Created (and Completed once done). A task that still carries an old Program shows it read-only as Program: … · retired, use Plan. Click a value to change it. A recurring checklist item shows Repeats in place of Deadline.
DependenciesWaiting on, Blocking and Related links to other tasks. Shown once something is linked (see below).
Sub-tasksThe child tasks, with their own owners and statuses, and a done/total count.
DocumentsLinks to outside files (Drive, Sheets, anything with a web address). Docket stores the link, not the file.
ActivityTwo tabs: Comments, with a box at the bottom to write a comment, and History, the full audit trail.

Sub-tasks and Documents are sections you can fold shut by clicking their headings.

Plan and hand-off properties

Two properties connect a task to the wider company, and both apply to top-level tasks only:

Plan

Click the value to search and pick a theme, milestone or result, or choose Unplanned to clear it. On a sub-task the field is read-only and shows the parent’s link, labelled from the parent task. See Linking Tasks to the Plan.

Hand-off to

Pick another team, and optionally a person in it. A status line reads Waiting for… to accept or Accepted by…, and the receiving team sees an Accept hand-off button here. You stay the owner. See Hand-offs.

Dependencies: waiting on, blocking, related

A dependency links two tasks so everyone can see what has to happen first. One link is shown from both ends: if DKT-12 is waiting on DKT-9, then DKT-9 shows as blocking DKT-12.

LinkWhat it means
Waiting onThis task cannot really finish until the other task is done. While at least one of those other tasks is still open, this task counts as waiting.
BlockingThe other end of the same link: other tasks are waiting for this one.
RelatedA plain cross-reference with no order and no rules. Useful for “see also”.

Links can join tasks in different spaces. Once you have linked at least one task, a Dependencies strip appears above the description, with a group for each kind (empty groups are hidden). Each row shows a status dot, the DKT- number, the title, the owner and the due date; click a row to open that task.

Adding a dependency

  1. Open the task and choose Add dependency… in the More actions (…) menu. Three other doors lead to the same place: the + Add button on the Dependencies strip, the + Dependency button beside the Description heading when nothing is linked yet, and ⌘K then Add dependency to DKT-… while the task is open.
  2. Pick the kind: Waiting on…, Blocks… or Related to….
  3. Search for the other task by title or DKT- number (two or more characters, in every space you can open) and press Enter or click it. Docket confirms with Linked DKT-….

To remove a link, click the x at the end of its row (Remove link). You need edit rights on the task you are working in. Both adding and removing are written to the History tab of both tasks (Added dependency, Removed dependency). When the last open blocker of a task is finished or abandoned, the waiting task gets an Unblocked line in its History.

Finished and abandoned blockers

A blocker counts as cleared once it is Done. An abandoned blocker also counts as cleared, but its row is tagged Blocker abandoned so the waiting owner knows the work was dropped, not completed. Cleared links stay on the strip as a record.

Marking a waiting task done

Docket warns you but does not stop you. If you mark a task done while it is still waiting on open tasks, a confirmation appears, for example DKT-9 is still waiting on: DKT-4 Print run. Mark done anyway? Confirm to finish it, or cancel to leave it as it is. The same warning appears when you tick it in the list, drag it on the board or use it in a bulk update (3 of these are waiting on open tasks. Mark all done anyway?).

Date clash hint

If a task is waiting on a blocker that is due after the task itself, the blocker’s row shows an amber line such as DKT-123 is due 30 Nov, after this task (25 Nov). It is only a hint. Docket never moves a date for you, because every deadline change needs a reason.

Tasks you can’t see

If a linked task lives in a space you cannot open, it appears only as 1 task you can’t see (or 3 tasks you can’t see). No title, number or owner is shown, but it still counts towards waiting.

What Docket refuses

You try to…Docket says
Make a loop (A waits on B, B waits on C, C waits on A)That would make a loop of tasks waiting on each other.
Link a task to itselfA task can’t depend on itself.
Link the same two tasks againThese two tasks are already linked.
Add a dependency to a recurring (checklist) taskRecurring tasks can’t have dependencies.
Change links on an abandoned task, or link to oneThis task is abandoned, so it’s read-only. / That task is abandoned. Pick an open one. Reactivate the task first to change its links.
Link to a task you cannot openYou can’t open that task, so you can’t link it.
ⓘ Waiting and Blocked are two different things

The Blocked status is still a manual choice you make in the Status picker; Docket never sets it for you, and a waiting task keeps whatever status it has. Nothing about a dependency changes a deadline or a status automatically. Reviewers can see links but not change them.

Editing

Every property is click-to-edit in the panel: click it, pick the new value, and it saves. The title and description save when you click away. You can only edit a task you own, created, or (as an admin) any task. Reviewers see all of this without the edit controls.

With focus outside a text box, these keys work inside an open task: Shift+S status, Shift+A owner, Shift+D deadline, Shift+P priority, s add a sub-task.

The deadline, and why it is locked

Under Deadline the panel shows the current date, and, once it has been moved, a REV tag with the number of revisions plus a line reading Original … · locked. The first date you set is the original promise and never changes. To move the deadline, open it and enter the new date and a required reason; the button reads Set the first time and Revise after that.

⛔ Abandoning is the only way to stop a task

There is no delete button anywhere in Docket. If a task should not be done, choose Abandon… (in the Status picker or the More actions menu) and give a reason; it is required and recorded. The task stays visible with a banner reading Abandoned and your reason. An abandoned task is read-only until it is reactivated: it cannot be edited, re-dated, re-parented, moved, commented on, or have collaborators or documents changed, and the server refuses any such change. The comment box is replaced by This task is abandoned — reactivate it to comment. You also cannot add a sub-task under it. Reactivating (a status change) is the one thing that works, and an admin can still delete a comment on it. The owner, creator or an admin can use the banner’s Reactivate button, which is also logged.

Comments and History

The Comments tab is a running discussion on the task. Type in the box at the bottom and press Comment; you can edit or delete your own comments. The History tab is the unchangeable record: every status change, every deadline revision (with its reason), every owner or priority change, every collaborator or document added or removed. You cannot edit history; that is the point of it.

✓ Share a task with a link

Use Copy link to send someone a direct link to the task; it opens on the full page. An address of the form /tasks?task=… opens the task over the Tasks list instead, which is also how Docket returns you to the list after you leave the full page. Either way the person only sees the task if they are allowed to see it.

ⓘ Moving a task to another space

The Space property lets the owner move a task into a different space, including a private one you belong to. Moving a task changes who can see it. Sub-tasks always follow their parent’s space.

chapters.title: The Task Lifecycle
chapters.html:
A task in Docket follows the same arc whatever the work is. Understanding that arc, and the few rules Docket enforces along the way, is the key to using it well. This chapter is the “why” behind the buttons.

The five statuses

Every task is in exactly one of five states. The first four you set yourself; the fifth has its own door.

StatusMeans
Not startedCaptured, but work hasn't begun.
In progressSomeone is actively working on it.
DoneFinished. Docket stamps the completion time.
BlockedStuck on something outside the owner's control, waiting on someone or something else.
AbandonedDeliberately stopped, with a reason. The only terminal end besides Done.

The arc of a task

  1. Captured. A title is typed and the task exists, sitting in The Grid as Not started.
  2. Set up. An owner and a deadline are added; it leaves the Grid and joins the main list.
  3. Worked. The owner moves it to In progress, adds collaborators, comments, documents and sub-tasks as needed.
  4. Finished or stopped. It becomes Done, or, if it should not be done at all, it is Abandoned with a reason. If it gets stuck, it sits at Blocked until it can move again.

The three things Docket will not let you fudge

Docket is intentionally strict about a few things, so the record stays trustworthy.

⛔ 1. The original deadline is locked

The first deadline put on a task becomes its locked original promise, and it never changes. To move the deadline afterwards you must revise it, which always asks for a short reason and records the change (old date → new date, with your reason) on the task's History. You can revise as many times as you need, but every slip is on the record. This is how Docket can always show whether work landed when it was first promised.

⛔ 2. Tasks are never deleted

There is no delete. A task you decide against is Abandoned, with a required reason, and stays visible marked as such. Nothing vanishes from the company's record, and an abandoned task can be reactivated if things change.

⛔ 3. The created date and creator are permanent

When a task was created, and by whom, can never be edited. So can the task's DKT- ID. These are anchors you can always trust.

Owner, creator, collaborators

Three kinds of people relate to a task, and they are not the same:

Owner

The single accountable person. There is exactly one. The owner can change every field and move the status.

Creator

Whoever first captured it, set automatically and never changed. The creator can also edit the task.

Collaborators

Helpers. They can comment, attach documents and add sub-tasks, but they do not change the owner, deadline or status. Many people can collaborate.

✓ One owner, on purpose

Docket gives every task exactly one owner so accountability is never split. If two people are doing the work, one owns it and the other is a collaborator. “Whose is this?” always has a one-name answer.

Sub-tasks

A task can be broken into sub-tasks, but only one level deep: a sub-task cannot have its own sub-tasks. New sub-tasks start by inheriting their parent's team and owner, which you can then change. Each is a full task in its own right with its own status and deadline; the parent shows a done/total count so you can see progress at a glance.

parts.subtitle: Themes, milestones and results; linking tasks to them; weeks and the on-time score; the weekly review; and handing tasks to another team.

chapters.title: Themes, Milestones & Results
chapters.html:
The Plan is where the company writes down what it is trying to achieve, in four levels, from a broad theme down to the everyday task. Linking your tasks to it answers a question the task list alone cannot: “does this work move one of our goals?”. The Plan sits above the task list; it never replaces it.

What it’s for
Goals, in four levels, with owners and dates.
Read or act?
Read for most people; Founders edit it.
Who
Member Founder Associate
Where
Plan at the top of the sidebar, or /plan.

The four levels

LevelWhat it isExample
ThemeA broad direction the company is working towards. Rarely changes.Grow online sales
MilestoneA dated outcome with one owner, inside a theme.M1 Launch the new website, owner Priya, due 30 Nov
ResultOne checkable piece of a milestone, with its own owner and date.M1.R1 Product pages are live
TaskThe daily work, exactly as you already know it. A task can be linked to a plan item.Write the copy for the home page

Each theme, milestone and result has a short code (such as M1 or M1.R1) so people can quote it. In the task pickers an item reads as a chain: Grow online sales › M1 › M1.R1.

The two ways to open it

Click Plan in the icon rail, or the first row of the sidebar. What you see depends on who you are:

Plan register

For Founders: every theme, with its milestones and results underneath, including targets and founders-only themes. Click any row to open it in a side panel and edit it. Founders add a theme with + Theme, a milestone with the Milestone button on a theme, and a result with Result on a milestone. The up and down arrows on a row change its order. A Founders’ Associate sees the same register read-only (no targets, no founders-only themes).

My milestones

For everyone else: the milestones you own, grouped under their theme, with the results beneath each. If a result of yours sits under someone else’s milestone, it appears in Results I own on other milestones. If you own nothing yet, you see You don’t own any milestones yet with a Propose button.

Each row shows the code, the title, the owner, the due date, a Re-dated tag if the date has moved, and a coloured state chip. A padlock marks a founders-only theme. The buttons at the top are Three weeks (see Plan Views), Propose (see Proposals, Measures & Targets) and, for Founders, + Theme.

States

Milestones and results move through a few states, shown as a chip on the row:

StateMeaning
ProposedA draft. Someone has suggested it, or a Founder has made it without agreeing it yet. The date is only a draft.
AgreedOwner, date and the “done when” sentence are settled. The due date is now locked (see below).
DoneFinished, with a line of evidence saying how we know.
DroppedDeliberately stopped, with a reason. Nothing is deleted.
SplitReplaced by two or more smaller ones (below). The original is greyed out and read-only, and points to its parts, for example Split → M4, M5.

A theme is simply Active or Retired.

ⓘ Nothing live under something closed

A milestone can only be agreed under a theme that is active, and a result only under an agreed milestone. You cannot drop or finish a milestone while results or tasks under it are still live; Docket tells you to drop or finish those first.

What you can do to an item

Open an item and the Actions row shows only what you are allowed to do in its current state.

ActionWhat it asks for
AgreeAn owner, a due date and a “done when” sentence. The due date locks.
Re-dateA new due date and a reason. See the note below.
Mark doneEvidence: what shows it is done, such as a link, a number or a note.
DropA reason.
ReopenA reason. Brings a done or dropped item back.
SplitFounders only. See below.

The panel also lists the item’s history (who did what, when, in Indian time) and the tasks linked to it that you can open.

⚠ Re-dating an agreed milestone needs a reason

Once a milestone is agreed, its due date cannot simply be edited. Use Re-date, pick the new date and write why. The original date is kept (the panel shows was 30 Nov), the row gets a Re-dated tag, and the move is recorded in the history and in the weekly review. This is the plan’s version of the audited task deadline.

Who can do what

  • Founders can do everything above, on every level.
  • The owner of a milestone can add results under it, and can edit, re-date and mark done the results under it. Changes to the milestone itself (agreeing, re-dating, finishing, dropping) are the Founders’.
  • The owner of a result can edit it and mark it done. Re-dating it, or changing its owner, is for the milestone’s owner or a Founder.
  • Everyone else reads, links their tasks, and proposes.

Splitting a milestone or result

When one agreed milestone turns out to be really two or three, a Founder uses Split instead of editing it. A split makes 2 to 10 new agreed parts and retires the original, all in one step:

  1. Give a reason, then fill in each part: title, owner and due date. Add or remove parts with the buttons beneath them.
  2. Decide where each result goes. Every live result under it is given to one of the parts, or dropped (with a reason for the dropped ones).
  3. Decide where the open tasks go. Pick a default part for linked open tasks, and override it for any task that belongs elsewhere. Tasks in spaces you cannot open go to the default part.
  4. Press Split. Everything moves together, and every item and task gets a history line. Done and abandoned tasks keep their old link.

Who sees what in the Plan

The Plan is deliberately not an open book. Everyone sees the shape of the company’s goals, but the targets and the detail stay with the people who need them.

You areYou see
Founder
(super admin)		Everything: every theme, milestone and result, the Target on each, and the founders-only themes.
Associate
(Founders’ Associate)		Every item that is not founders-only, in full, except targets. Read-only.
An ownerThe milestones you own and the results under them, plus the title of every theme that is not founders-only. No targets.
Everyone elseThe title of every theme that is not founders-only. Nothing below it unless you own it.

A founders-only (restricted) theme is marked with a padlock and is invisible to everyone except Founders, together with everything under it. Founders switch it on with the Restricted tick box on the theme.

ⓘ Linking to someone else’s milestone

You can link your task to a milestone you do not own only if you can see it. If a task you can open is linked to a milestone you cannot see, its chip simply reads Another owner’s milestone, and hovering shows only the theme. A task linked to a founders-only item shows no plan chip at all to anyone outside that circle.

ⓘ The Founders’ space

Tasks linked to a founders-only item live in a special Founders’ space that only the Founders can open. Its tasks are never named in a Slack message, a copied review summary or anyone else’s list. Other people only ever see them as a count, such as “+3 in spaces you’re not in”.

chapters.title: Proposals, Measures & Targets
chapters.html:
If something belongs on the plan and is not there, anyone can say so. A proposal goes to the Founders, who accept or decline it, and you always find out which, and why. This chapter also covers how a milestone says it is measured, and the one place Docket nudges a Founder to close something off.

What it’s for
Raising a milestone or a risk; measuring one.
Who proposes
Anyone with a Docket login.
Who decides
Founder
Where
Propose button on /plan

Proposing something

  1. Press Propose at the top of the Plan page. A panel opens on the right.
  2. Fill it in. What (a short title) and Why it matters are required; the Founders read the why when they decide. Under It is a… choose Milestone: something to deliver or Risk: something that could go wrong. Theme and By when are optional hints.
  3. Press Send proposal. You can have up to 20 waiting at a time.

Your proposals appear under My proposals on the Plan page, each marked Waiting, Accepted or Declined. A declined one shows the Founders’ reason. You only ever see your own proposals, and the code of an accepted milestone only if you are allowed to see that milestone.

Deciding on proposals Founder

Founders see a Proposed section on the Plan page with a count of what is waiting (Nothing waiting. when clear), followed by the decisions of the last 30 days. Open one to read what, why, who and when, and any suggested theme, owner or date, then choose:

Accept

Tick Create a milestone for it to turn it into a real milestone: pick the Theme, edit the Milestone title, pick the Owner, and either leave it a draft or tick Agreed now (which asks for a due date and a done-when sentence and locks the date). Leave the tick off to simply note it; a note is then required. A risk with no milestone created is noted and closed.

Decline

A reason is required, and the proposer sees it.

The weekly review also lists what was proposed that week and how many are still waiting (see The Weekly Review).

“Done when” and how it is measured

Every agreed milestone and result has a Done when sentence, a plain statement of what finished looks like. Beside it is Done when · measured from, which says how Docket can check it:

  • Not measured: nobody will check it automatically; a person decides.
  • Or pick a system, then a metric from that system, then type a target such as ≥ 97% for 4 weeks.

Founders also keep a separate Target note on each item. Targets are visible only to Founders.

The ⚠ No data source chip

An amber ⚠ No data source chip on a milestone or result means no system records this today, so it will be checked by hand. It appears on a live item that:

  • is agreed but has no measure at all,
  • is set to “manual”, or
  • names a metric that no system records yet.

A draft proposal is not flagged until it has a measure. The chip is a prompt to fix the plan, not an error; the review and the re-plan list these as warnings.

The reading chip

When a metric can be read automatically, Docket checks it every morning and shows the latest reading on the row, such as 92% · 30d to 12 Nov: the value over the last 30 days. A target reached mark appears beside it when the target is met. A target that is a ceiling (“at most”) is only judged once the due date arrives, so it never shows as reached early.

Target reached: confirm done Founder

When an agreed item’s reading meets its target, a Target reached — confirm done section appears at the top of the Plan page for Founders, with a count. Each row shows the code, title, the reading, the metric and the target. Press Mark done and the normal done form opens with the evidence already filled in from the reading; edit it if you like and confirm.

✓ Docket never closes it for you

A reached target only nudges a Founder. The item stays agreed until a person confirms it is done.

chapters.title: Plan Views: Three Weeks, Tree, Templates, Re-plan
chapters.html:
Besides the register itself, the Plan has four more screens, each answering a different question: Three weeks (what is due soon, and what needs a hand), Tree (how each goal is progressing), Templates (reusable plans) and Re-plan (is next month ready). They sit in the sidebar under Plan.

What it’s for
Looking at the plan by time, by goal, and by month.
Read or act?
Mostly read; Templates act.
Who
Member Founder Associate
Always cut to you
Every screen shows only what you may see.

Who can open which

ScreenAddressWho
Plan/planEveryone (the register for Founders, read-only for Associates, My milestones for the rest).
Three weeks/plan/weeksEveryone.
Tree/plan/treeEveryone.
Templates/plan/templatesAnyone who may make a template, or who can see one. The sidebar row appears only then.
Re-plan/plan/replanFounders only. The sidebar row appears only for them; anyone else who opens the address sees Founders only.

Three weeks

A rolling window of Overdue, This week, Next week and Week after. Each cell lists the milestones and results due in that week (a target icon, code, title and date) and the tasks due that week (a status dot, the title, the owner and date). Click a task to open it.

Rows

The Team | Person | Theme switch chooses what the rows are.

Team

Pick All teams or one team. Founders start on all teams; everyone else starts on their own team.

Warnings

Above the grid, four kinds of warning, each saying who needs to act (For Priya, For the founders). When there are none you see No warnings.

WarningWhat it means
No actionable tasksAn agreed item is due in the window and has no open task with both an owner and a date.
Not agreed yetA proposed milestone is due in the window.
Linked to a theme onlyAn open task is linked to a theme that now has agreed milestones, so it should be pointed at one. If you can edit the task, a Link to a milestone button fixes it in one click.
StaleNo update or comment for 3 or more working days.

Only top-level tasks appear. Founders also see +N in spaces you’re not in where open tasks sit in spaces they cannot open. With nothing due you see Nothing due in the next three weeks.

Tree

The whole plan as a tree: theme, milestone, result, task. Click a row to fold it open or shut. Under each plan item Docket shows counts for everything beneath it (12 open, 5 done, 2 overdue) and an on time % that compares finished tasks against their first deadline (recurring checklist work is left out).

  • Theme picks one theme or All themes; Mine only shows the items you own and the path down to them; Show closed adds done and dropped items; Expand all and Collapse all do what they say.
  • Tasks hang directly under the item they are linked to, up to 25; a +N more link opens the Tasks list filtered to that item. Click a task to open it.
  • If you cannot see an item’s parent, it hangs under the nearest one you can see. Founders also see +N hidden where tasks sit in spaces they cannot open.

Templates

A template is a reusable plan: a list of steps (milestones, results and tasks), each with a Role (such as “Lead”) and a Day offset from a start date. A launch, a hiring round or a monthly close are typical. Applying one creates everything in one go.

The list

Each template has Apply and, if it is yours, Edit (otherwise Preview). Show archived includes retired ones; New template starts one. With none, the screen says No templates yet.

Two kinds

Founders: under a theme, made by Founders, which create milestones, results and tasks under a theme; and Leads: under a milestone, which anyone who owns an agreed milestone or result can make, and which is applied under a milestone you own.

Editing

Name, optional description, who it is for, then the Steps. Each step has a title, a Role and a Day (0 is the start date, a negative number is before it; the screen spells it out, such as 3 days before). Add a milestone, result or task step where it belongs, reorder with the arrows, and press Save. Archive retires it.

Applying

Pick the theme or milestone to apply it under, the Anchor date (day 0), and who plays each role. A preview titled What will be created lists every item with its date and person. Press Apply; the result reads Applied “name” with how many plan items and tasks were created.

ⓘ Applying follows the normal rules

Created items go through the same checks as ones made by hand: spaces still decide who can have a task, and a task linked to a founders-only item is created in the Founders’ space.

Re-plan Founder

The monthly check that next month is ready to start. The title reads Re-plan · Month Year and defaults to next month; use the arrows or Next month to move.

  • Readiness: one row per milestone due that month, with ticks for Agreed, Owner, Data source and Tasks (first 2 wks) (how many actionable tasks are lined up for the first fortnight), and an overall Ready mark. The header counts how many are ready and not ready. Filter by Team; Not ready first floats the gaps to the top.
  • Risks: the risks people have proposed since the last re-plan.
  • Scores: the on-time percentage for each team for each week of the month just closed.

The screen is read-only. Getting a row ready means doing the work elsewhere (agree the milestone, give it an owner, add tasks) and coming back.

chapters.title: Linking Tasks to the Plan
chapters.html:
A task becomes part of the plan by being linked to a theme, milestone or result. The link is just one more field on the task, but it is what lets the weekly review say how much of the week’s work was planned. Linking is optional; a task with no link is called Unplanned.

What it’s for
Tying a task to a goal.
Read or act?
Act: set or clear the Plan field.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Applies to
Top-level tasks only.

Where to set it

PlaceHow
Inside a taskThe Plan property. Click it, search, and pick. Unplanned at the top clears the link.
New task formA Plan field that starts as Unplanned; type to search for a theme, milestone or result.
Quick captureA Plan chip beside Owner, Deadline and Priority on the capture line. It only appears when there is something for you to link to.
The listThe Plan column (turn it on in Columns). Click a cell and pick; an empty cell offers Set plan.
The BoardCards show the plan chip. Set the link from the card’s task view.

The picker lists what you may link to, each as a chain such as Grow online sales › M1 › M1.R1 · Product pages are live, and it searches codes, theme names and words in titles. You can link to a proposed or agreed item; closed ones are not offered.

What is shown on the task

The chip shows the item’s code; hover for its title. A chip reading Another owner’s milestone means the link goes to a milestone you cannot see (hover shows its theme only). A task with no link shows nothing in the list and Unplanned in the task view.

⚠ Top-level tasks only: sub-tasks inherit

A sub-task cannot carry its own link. It shows its parent’s link in grey, labelled from the parent task; to change it, change the parent. A sub-task of an unlinked parent reads Follows the parent task.

Filtering by plan

Open Filter on the Tasks list and use the Plan picker (default Any plan):

  • Pick a theme to see every task under it, including its milestones and results.
  • Pick a milestone to see tasks linked to it or to its results.
  • Pick a result to see only its own tasks.
  • Pick Unplanned to see the tasks with no link at all, the list to work through before a review.

Links in the Plan, the Tree and the review (+N more) open the Tasks list already filtered this way.

Who may link what

You can edit the Plan field on a task you may edit, and link it to an item you can see. Founders can link to anything. A task linked to a founders-only item must sit in the Founders’ space, so Docket will not let anyone else link one. Moving a task out of the Founders’ space is a Founders-only action.

ⓘ Programs are retired

The plan link replaces the old Program label. Tasks that already carried a program keep it, shown read-only and marked as retired. Nothing sets a program any more.

chapters.title: Weeks and Week Ending
chapters.html:
Docket thinks in weeks as well as days. Every task with a deadline belongs to a “week ending” date, and the list, the grid and the board can group and filter by it. This is the same week the on-time score and the weekly review use, so what you see in the list matches what gets reviewed.

What it’s for
Seeing and planning work by week.
Read or act?
Read: grouping and filtering only.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Where
Group and Filter on the Tasks list and board.

What a week is

A week runs from midnight to midnight in Indian time and is named by its last day, the week ending date. A task belongs to the week that contains its effective deadline: the revised deadline if it has been revised, otherwise the original one.

Three company-wide settings define the calendar:

SettingStarts asUsed for
Week ending daySundayWhere one week stops and the next begins.
Working daysMonday to SaturdayCounting “3 working days” for stale warnings and for the review’s quiet-day check.
HolidaysNoneDays that do not count as working days.

The founders decide these for the whole company; there is no screen for changing them yet, so ask the Docket owner. A later change never rewrites weeks that have already been scored.

Group by Week ending

Open the Group button on the toolbar and choose Week ending. The list reflows into groups:

  • Overdue first, then one group per Week ending date in order, and No date last.
  • The Board offers the same choice and turns each of those groups into a column.

The Week filter

In the Filter panel, Week narrows the list to one week. It works on the List, the Grid and the Board, and on My tasks.

ChoiceShows
Any weekNo week filter (the default).
This weekTasks due in the current week, including ones in it that are already past their time.
Next weekTasks due in the following week.
Week ending…Pick any day; Docket snaps it to its week and shows the resulting week ending date beside the picker.
OverdueThe same as the existing Overdue filter: open tasks whose deadline has passed.
No dateTasks with no deadline yet.
⚠ The Board’s week columns are read-only

With the Board grouped by Week ending you cannot drag a card from one week to another, and the columns have no add line. A deadline never moves by a drag. To move a deadline, open the task and Revise it with a reason (see Inside a Task). The first deadline is set freely; every later change is recorded with its reason, which is what keeps the weekly score honest.

✓ A weekly habit

Before a review, filter to This week, then Next week, and set an owner and a deadline on anything missing. Then filter the Plan to Unplanned and link what should be linked.

chapters.title: The On-time Score
chapters.html:
The on-time score says, for each team and each week, what share of the tasks people promised to finish that week were finished by the time they promised. It is deliberately fixed in advance: the list of promises is frozen when the week starts, so a score cannot be improved by quietly moving dates afterwards.

What it’s for
Measuring promises kept, by team, by week.
Read or act?
Read only. Nothing to enter.
Who sees it
In the Weekly Review, cut to your access.
Counted in
Top-level, non-recurring tasks.

The cohort: what is counted

The week’s cohort is the list of tasks the score is about. It is taken at the very start of the week (just after midnight Indian time at the start of the week) and includes every open, top-level task whose deadline falls in that week. Recurring checklist items and sub-tasks are not part of it. The task’s deadline, team and owner as they were at that moment are frozen, so moving a task to another team later does not change whose score it is.

Joining mid-week

  • A task joins the week if it is given its first deadline inside the week: a new task created with a deadline this week, or an undated task dated for the first time.
  • A task created already done within the week counts as on time.
  • Re-dating a task into the week does not add it. If it slipped from an earlier week, that was the earlier week’s miss.
  • Re-dating a task out of the week does not remove it.

What counts as on time

OutcomeWhen
On timeAt the close of the week the task is done and was completed at or before the deadline it was committed with.
MissedAnything else in the cohort: still open, done late, re-dated and finished after the original time, abandoned during the week (a dropped promise is a miss), or done and then reopened and not finished again.

The score is on time ÷ committed, per team. For example, 18 of 20 committed tasks done in time is 90%.

Provisional and final

While the week is running, the review shows a PROVISIONAL score: how many were committed, how many are on time so far, how many have missed so far (their time has already passed) and how many are still due. The week closes at the end of its last day, and the score becomes FINAL and is stored unchanged. Opening and closing can lag by a few minutes. A week that was opened late says opened late, not exact; scores are exact from the week that began on 16 November 2026.

Who can see the score

There is no score on the task list or the dashboard. It is read in the Weekly Review (see the next chapters), and you see only what your access allows:

You areYou see
A team member or leadYour own team’s score, counting only tasks you can open.
AssociateAny team’s score, counting only tasks they can open.
FounderAny team, or all teams, with every task counted. Tasks in spaces they cannot open are included in the numbers and shown only as +N in spaces you’re not in.
ⓘ Why a deadline can’t be edited quietly

The first deadline is free to set; every later change goes through Revise with a reason, and is the only way the date moves. The review shows each slipped task with its original date, its new one, how many times it moved and the reasons given.

chapters.title: The Weekly Review
chapters.html:
The Weekly Review is one page that tells a team how its week went and what is coming: the score, what slipped and why, milestones due, who has gone quiet, and the next two weeks. It is built fresh from the live tasks, so a Thursday glance and a Friday meeting read from the same source. A second page, Founders’ catch-up, is for the Founders’ own weekly conversation.

What it’s for
Reviewing the week and the next two.
Read or act?
Read; Founders can Hold and set a top 5.
Who
Member Founder Associate
Where
Review in the sidebar, /review

The page

The title reads Review · week ending a date, with a PROVISIONAL or FINAL tag and an As of… time in Indian time.

Week stepper

Left and right arrows step a week at a time; This week jumps back. A week that has not started yet says Not started yet, and a week that was never opened says This week has no score.

Team picker

Founders and Associates choose All teams or one team. Everyone else sees their own team only. If your profile has no team you see No team on your profile; ask an admin.

Copy for Slack

Copies a ready-to-paste text summary of what is on screen. It never names a task from the Founders’ space or a founders-only milestone, whoever copies it. It is greyed out until the week has a score.

Hold Founder

Stores the provisional view as a snapshot, so the minutes of a meeting can point at exactly what was on screen (Held). Snapshots lists the stored versions for the week; open one to read it as it was, and press Back to live to return. The final score is stored automatically when the week closes.

What is in the pack

For each team there is one card with these sections, in this order:

SectionWhat it shows
This weekCommitted, on time, missed so far (or missed), still due, and the on-time percentage, marked provisional or final. See The On-time Score.
Last weekThe same for the week before, plus a small chart of the last four weeks.
SlippedEach task that missed: its owner, the committed date against the current date, how many times it moved, and every revision with its reason and when.
MilestonesMilestones due this week and whether each is done; any re-dated this week, with the reason; and warnings: no actionable tasks, no data source, not agreed.
Hand-offsHand-offs that are Overdue or Unowned (no one named, or not accepted, in the next two weeks). See Hand-offs.
StalenessFor each person with open committed tasks, how recently they updated things and the share they touched. This week only, a banner reads Quiet on…, no update on any open task if the last working day was silent. Only Founders see when a colleague was last in Docket.
Next two weeksThe milestones due, then the tasks due, grouped by person.
UnplannedHow many committed tasks have no plan link, for example 3 of 20 committed tasks have no plan link (15%). See Linking Tasks to the Plan.

Founders also get a Proposals card at the bottom (how many are waiting, and what was submitted this week), and, above the pack, a Score trend chart: on time, week by week, for the last closed weeks. It starts to draw once two weeks have closed (The trend starts after two closed weeks).

ⓘ Cut to the reader, always

The pack is built for whoever opens it. A team lead sees their own team and only the tasks they can open. Founders see every team with every task counted, and tasks in spaces they cannot open appear as +N in spaces you’re not in. A held snapshot is cut to the reader again when it is opened.

Founders’ catch-up Founder

Open Founders’ catch-up in the sidebar (or the button at the top of the Review). Anyone else who opens it sees Founders only. It has a week stepper, a Review button back, and its own Copy for Slack. It holds three things:

Cross-team asks

Open top-level tasks due this week or next that are waiting on a task owned by another team. Each ask shows the waiting task, waiting on, and the task it waits for, with the team, owner and date of each. This is where blocked cross-team work gets noticed.

Hand-offs between teams

Open hand-offs due this week or next that no one has accepted or been named for.

Top 5

Each Founder’s five most important things for the week, in rank order. Your own card is editable: each slot can hold a Plan item or a Task (use the buttons) and a note, or just a free-text note. Press Save; empty slots are left out. The other Founder’s card is read-only. Once a week is over its top 5 is a record and cannot be changed.

chapters.title: Hand-offs
chapters.html:
Sometimes your task needs someone on another team to take it forward: design needs to produce the artwork, finance needs to approve the payment. A hand-off sends the task to that team (and optionally to a named person) and makes sure someone says “I have it”. Until they do, the task is flagged, and the weekly review notices.

What it’s for
Passing a task to another team, with an accept.
Read or act?
Act: give, and accept.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Applies to
Top-level tasks only.

Giving a task to another team

  1. Open the task and find Hand-off to in the properties (you need edit rights, and it must be a top-level task, not a sub-task).
  2. Pick the team. Any team except the task’s own; the first choice, Not a hand-off, removes it again.
  3. Optionally name a person. A second picker appears beside the team, reading Anyone in <team>. Choose a person in that team, or leave it open for the team to sort out.

A status line then reads Waiting for Design to accept (or Design/Asha if you named someone). A small chip such as → Design appears on the task’s row, grid card and board card, in amber until it is accepted.

ⓘ The task stays yours

You remain the owner and the deadline is the hand-off date. The receiving team does not take the task over; it confirms it has picked it up. Changing the team or the named person clears an acceptance, so the new receiver has to accept again.

Incoming: what has been handed to you

On My tasks an Incoming section appears above your groups whenever hand-offs are addressed to you or your team. It stays hidden when there are none. A number beside the heading counts the ones not yet accepted.

  • Two tabs split them: To you (you are the named person) and To your team (everyone else in the receiving team).
  • Each row shows the status dot, task number and title, from the giver and their team, who it is to, and the due date. Click it to open the task.
  • The right-hand end shows Accept if you may accept, accepted once someone has, or waiting if it is not yours to accept.

You can see a hand-off task that is in the open General space even if you would not normally see that team’s tasks. A hand-off in a private space is visible only to members of that space.

Accepting

The named person, or anyone in the receiving team when no one is named, can accept; the giver cannot accept their own hand-off. Accept from the Incoming row, or press Accept hand-off beside Hand-off to inside the task.

What changes when you accept

  • The status line changes to Accepted by … with the date, and the row chip loses its amber colour.
  • If no person was named, you are recorded as the receiver.
  • The task leaves the Unowned hand-off lists in the weekly review and the Founders’ catch-up.
  • History records Hand-off accepted. The owner and the deadline do not change.
⚠ Only an open task can be accepted

Docket says This task is closed if it is already done or abandoned, and This task isn’t a hand-off any more if the giver has cleared it in the meantime.

parts.subtitle: Spaces: private, walled-off areas for tasks. (Programs are retired; the Plan replaces them.)

chapters.title: Spaces
chapters.html:
A Space is a private, walled-off area for tasks. Only its members can see what is inside, even admins are shut out unless they are added. Everything that is not in a private space lives in the open General space, which is where the company's day-to-day work sits.

What it is
A hard visibility boundary around tasks.
Affects access?
Yes, this is its whole point.
Who can make one
Anyone; you become its owner.
Per task
Always exactly one space.

General: the open default
