General is the single open space everyone shares. Every task that was around before spaces existed lives here, and so does anything you capture without choosing a space. Inside General, the normal visibility rules apply: you see your own, your collaborators' and your own department's tasks; reviewers and admins see everything. General cannot be renamed, archived, or deleted, it is always there.

Private spaces: the wall

A private space is the opposite of General: nobody can see it or anything in it unless they are a member. This is the strongest rule in Docket.

⛔ A private space beats even Admin

Being an Admin or a Reviewer does not get you into a private space. If you are not a member, the space and its tasks are invisible to you, they do not appear in lists, search, the dashboard, or anywhere else. The only sanctioned way an admin can enter is the audited break-glass recovery (covered in the admin chapter), and that act is logged. Spaces are for genuinely confidential work.

Inside a private space, visibility is flat: every member sees every task in it, there is no department sub-filtering like in General. If you are in the space, you see all of it.

Creating and using a space

  1. Create it with + New then New space in the top bar, or the + beside Spaces in the sidebar. Give it a name and create it. You become its owner and first member.
  2. It appears in your sidebar under My spaces (spaces you own); a space someone else added you to appears under By others. Click it to see only that space's tasks; anything you capture while inside it lands there.
  3. Add members from the space's settings (the settings button at the right of the views bar, shown to the space’s owner). Only people with a Docket login can be added.
  4. Move existing tasks in using the Space property in the task view, or Move in the bulk bar.

Owning a space

The space's owner (and only the owner) can, from the space settings:

Rename

Change the space's name.

Members

Add or remove people. Only employees with a login can be members.

Transfer ownership

Hand the space to another member, for example before leaving the team.

Archive

Retire the space. It leaves the sidebar, but its tasks are kept.

Within a private space, a task can be edited by its owner, its creator, or the space owner, so the person running the space can keep its tasks tidy.

ⓘ Each space has its own dashboard

From the views bar of a private space, the dashboard icon opens a dashboard scoped to just that space, the same tiles and breakdowns as the org dashboard, but only counting that space's tasks. Any member can view it.

⚠ If a space's owner leaves

If a space is orphaned (its owner is gone and nobody else can manage it), an admin can step in through the break-glass recovery on the admin Spaces screen, which makes them the owner and is recorded. The everyday answer, though, is to transfer ownership before the owner leaves.

ⓘ Programs are retired

Docket used to have a second grouping, Programs, a soft label that gathered tasks from many spaces. It has been retired: there is no Programs section in the sidebar, no way to add a program to a task, and nothing to create. Tasks that already had one keep it, shown read-only. To tie tasks together by purpose, link them to the Plan instead (see Linking Tasks to the Plan). An old program link still opens a read-only list of its tasks.

parts.subtitle: Your recurring work: routines you tick off on a repeat schedule, kept separate from the task board.

chapters.title: Checklists
chapters.html:
Checklists are your recurring work: the things you do every day, every Monday, or on the first of the month, that don’t deserve a fresh task each time. You set them up once with a repeat schedule, and they show up on your own checklist whenever they’re due, ready to tick off.

What it’s for
Routine, repeating work you tick off.
Whose it is
One person’s checklist at a time.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Find it
Checklist on the icon rail.

Checklists vs Tasks

A normal task happens once and has a deadline. A checklist item happens again and again on a schedule and has no deadline, just a repeat rule. Because of that, checklist items are kept completely separate from the Tasks board:

ⓘ Recurring work stays off the board

Checklist items never appear on the Tasks list or the Dashboard, and they don’t count toward anyone’s task totals. They live only on the /checklist page. If you open one in the task view it shows Repeats (its schedule) where a task would show a deadline.

The layout

The Checklist screen has three tabs along the top: My day, Manage and Oversight. Under each, work is grouped under collapsible headers, the same style as the Tasks list.

My day

What is due on the day you are viewing. The Today group lists every item due, ready to tick, with a done count (for example 3/5). Below it come any checklist templates assigned to you, and a Recurring this week group previewing the rest of this week’s items with the days they fall on (read-only: you tick an item on its own day). Arrows beside the date step back to earlier days; the Today button brings you back. A Today | Register switch at the top flips the same checklist into a chart (see The Register below).

Manage

Where you set things up. My recurring tasks lists every recurring item you own with its schedule, and a New button to add one. Checklist templates below it holds reusable multi-section checklists for a role, with a New template button.

Oversight

For managers: per-person checklist adherence for a chosen date, covering people you manage or have assigned a checklist to. Click a person to see their run for that day, read-only.

Managers and reviewers who can view other people’s checklists also get a person picker on My day, to see how a report is tracking (read-only, see below).

Creating a checklist item

  1. Open Manage and click New. Give the item a title (e.g. “Check the cold-storage temperature log”), and optionally set who it is assigned to, its priority, team and a description.
  2. Choose how often it repeats with the schedule picker: Daily, Weekly (tick the weekdays, e.g. Mon, Wed, Fri) or Monthly (a day of the month; in shorter months it falls on the last day).
  3. Set a time of day. The time it should be done by, used only to order your day, it doesn’t nag you.
  4. Click Add. From now on it appears under Today whenever the schedule says it’s due.
✓ Optional end date

The schedule picker has an optional Ends date. Set one for a routine that should only run for a while (a temporary daily check during a launch, say), and the item auto-drops off your checklist once that date passes, no need to remember to retire it.

To change a schedule later, click the pencil beside the item in Manage. It opens the same schedule picker as a small popover; choose the new pattern and click Save.

Ticking things off

On the My day tab, tick the item to mark it done for that day; the progress count goes up and the tick sticks across reloads (it records a completion for that date). Made a mistake? Un-tick it and the completion is removed. Each day is its own slate, ticking today has no effect on yesterday or tomorrow.

The Register

At the top of My day is a Today | Register switch; Docket remembers your choice on this device. Today is the list described above. Register is a paper-style chart: your items run down the left, the dates they were due run across the top, and each item gets one cell per day. It shows the same ticks as Today, so ticking in either view is the same tick.

Window

7D, 14D or 30D (it opens on 14D). Use the ‹ › arrows to page back and forward, and Today to jump back. You can never page past today. Only dates on which at least one item was due become columns, so a Monday-only weekly item shows just Mondays.

Cells

Green tick: done. Amber tick: done late (after the section’s due time, or the task’s set time). Hollow tick: ticked later, filled in on a later day; it still counts, but the chart shows it was back-filled. Red cross: missed (due, the day is over, not ticked). Empty box: due today, not ticked yet. Dot: not scheduled that day. Hover a cell to see when it was ticked and by whom (on shared charts, also who it was done for).

Adherence

A percentage at the end of every row (that item), a number at the foot of every column (that day), and the chart’s overall percentage with done/due in its header. Today only counts once ticked, because the day isn’t over. Green is 90 and above, amber 60 to 89, red below 60.

Blocks

One block per chart: Recurring tasks (your own recurring tasks) first, then every checklist template assigned to you.

A tick is never lost when an item’s schedule changes later: a past tick on a day the new schedule skips still shows, and still counts, on that day.

Ticking from the Register: click a cell on your own checklist, for today or any past day the item was due. Un-tick the same way. Future days can never be ticked, on either view (the server refuses it too), and neither can a day the item isn’t scheduled.

ⓘ Viewing someone else’s Register

Managers and Reviewers who can view a person’s checklist through the person selector see that person’s Register too, read-only.

Shared charts

A checklist template normally gives each assigned person their own chart. In Manage, the template editor has a Chart setting: Each person their own (the default) or One shared chart. A shared chart is one chart for a place or a line (a washroom, say): whoever is assigned ticks it, and the tick records who. Shared charts carry a Shared chart tag on My day and in the Register.

On a shared chart an assignee can type a name into “Ticking for someone? Name them” before ticking. This is for a supervisor ticking on behalf of floor staff who have no Docket login; the cell then shows “for <name>” on hover. Only the person who ticked it, or the checklist’s creator or an admin, can clear a shared tick: a tick is the record. A shared cell someone else ticked shows as read-only for the other assignees. If two people tick the same shared item at the same moment, the first tick stands.

ⓘ The Chart setting locks once used

A checklist’s Chart setting (own or shared) can’t be switched once anything on it has been ticked.

Assigning a checklist item to someone else

You can create a checklist item for another person, it lands on their checklist, not yours, and they tick it off. Use this to hand someone a recurring responsibility (a daily open/close routine, a weekly stock check).

⚠ Only the owner ticks their own items

A manager or reviewer can open a report’s checklist through the person picker to see how they’re doing, but cannot tick items on their behalf, the person who owns the item is the only one who marks it done. (Shared charts are the exception: any assignee ticks them.) This keeps a checklist an honest record of what that person actually completed.

Editing & retiring

Click an item’s title to open it and change its title or details, or use the pencil in Manage to change the schedule. When a routine is no longer needed, use Stop (the circle-slash button) in Manage. It asks for a reason, works like abandoning a task, and the item stops appearing under Today; the history of what was completed is kept.

parts.subtitle: Your own private notebook with a built-in calculator.

chapters.title: Scratchpad
chapters.html:
The Scratchpad is your own private notebook inside Docket: a place for rough notes, lists and quick sums that belong to nobody but you. It is not a task, not shared, and not tracked, just somewhere to think.

What it’s for
Your private notes and quick maths.
Who can see it
Only you. Always.
Who
Member Reviewer Admin
Saving
Automatic, as you type.

Strictly yours

⛔ Nobody else can read your Scratchpad, not even an admin

Scratchpad notes are tied to you and to you alone. There is no admin view, no sharing, no recovery path into them. This is deliberate, so it is a safe place for rough drafts and half-thoughts. The flip side: there is no undo, a deleted note is gone for good.

The layout

On a computer the Scratchpad has up to three columns:

Notes column (left)

All your notes, with a count. The + beside the heading creates a new note; click any note to open it. Each note shows its title, or its first line if you haven’t titled it. A reminder at the bottom says the notes are private to you.

Editor (middle)

A Title box and a large free-text area for the open note. Beside the title are two buttons: a calculator button that shows or hides the calculator, and a bin to delete the note.

Calculator (right)

Shown while a note is open. Hide it with the calculator button if you want the full width for writing; Docket remembers your choice.

On a phone the notes column and the editor take turns. Tap a note to open it, and tap ‹ Notes at the top left of the editor to go back to the list.

Writing notes

Type anything in the note area, plain free text. Your changes save automatically a moment after you stop typing (and when you switch notes or leave the page), there is no save button. To title a note, fill in the title box at the top; otherwise its first line stands in. To remove a note, use the bin icon next to the title (it asks you to confirm, because there is no undo).

The calculator

Beside an open note sits a real calculator for quick sums while you think, no need to leave Docket or open another app. Type a sum into its display, or tap the on-screen keypad, and the result shows live underneath as you go. It understands the everyday things, plus, minus, times, divide, brackets and percentages:

You typeYou get
120 * 4 + 50530
1200 * 18%216  (18% of 1200)
(90 + 60) / 350

A trailing percentage like 18% is treated as “eighteen hundredths”, so 1200 * 18% gives the tax on 1200. Press Enter (or the = key) to collapse the sum down to its result, so you can carry on from the answer. C clears the display.

✓ Keyboard flow

While writing a note, press Tab to jump straight into the calculator, and Shift+Tab to jump back to your note. You can do a quick sum and return to typing without touching the mouse.

ⓘ What the Scratchpad is not

Notes are not tasks. Nothing here shows up on the board, the dashboard or anyone's list, and the calculator works one sum at a time (it doesn't remember running totals between lines). If a note turns into real work, capture it as a task on the Tasks list so it has an owner and a deadline.

parts.subtitle: The org-wide review surface, and how to share it.

chapters.title: The Dashboard
chapters.html:
The Dashboard is the bird's-eye view of work across the whole company: how much is overdue, how much is due soon, and how it breaks down by team and by person. It is the screen founders and reviewers open first, and it can be shared with anyone who needs the overview.

What it’s for
The org-wide health of all tasks.
Read or act?
Read-only: a review surface.
Who
Reviewer Admin + anyone it’s shared with
Covers
All tasks in the General space.

The summary cards

Five summary cards run across the top. Two of them (Overdue and Revised) are clickable shortcuts into the matching task list.

TileWhat it counts
Overdue (red)Tasks whose deadline has passed and aren't done. Click to see them.
Due ≤ 7 daysTasks due within the coming week, your near-term pressure.
OpenEverything still in flight (not done, not abandoned).
Done (30d) (green)Tasks completed in the last 30 days, recent throughput.
RevisedTasks whose deadline has been moved at least once. Click to see them.
✓ The “revised” tile is a slippage gauge

Because the original deadline is always locked, the Deadline revised count is a direct measure of how often promises are moving. A rising number is an early warning that plans are slipping, well before things actually go overdue.

Status distribution

A single coloured bar shows how all tasks split across the five statuses, Not started, In progress, Done, Blocked, Abandoned, each status taking a share of the bar by its count (hover a segment to see the number), with a legend and the exact counts beneath. It tells you at a glance whether work is moving or piling up.

By team and by person

Two tables break the same work down by who owns it:

  • By team, one row per department, with Open / Done / Overdue counts. Click a row to jump to that team's tasks.
  • By person, one row per owner, with the same counts plus a Last seen time (when they were last active in Docket) and a small Load bar comparing their done and open work. Click a row to see that person's tasks.

An overdue count greater than zero is shown in red, so the teams and people under pressure stand out.

Who can open the Dashboard

Dashboard access is separate from everything else. Three kinds of people can open it:

Reviewer

Anyone who can see all org tasks gets the Dashboard automatically.

Admin

Always.

Granted

Anyone an admin shares it with, even a plain Member, either by turning on “visible to everyone” or by being named individually. See the admin Roles & Permissions chapter.

ⓘ Seeing the dashboard isn’t seeing every task

If you've been granted the Dashboard but are otherwise a Member, you see the full org-wide numbers, but clicking through to a list still shows only the tasks you're normally allowed to see (your own, your team's, the ones you collaborate on). The overview is shared; the detail stays scoped to you. This is intended.

⚠ If you reach a “no access” message

If the Dashboard says you don't have access, it simply hasn't been shared with you. Ask an admin to add you on the Roles & Permissions screen.

parts.subtitle: Roles, who has which role, dashboard sharing, and the space registry. Admins only.

chapters.title: Roles & Permissions
chapters.html:
Roles & permissions is where admins decide what kinds of access exist in Docket, and, on the same screen, who can see the Dashboard. It is the control room for access.

What it’s for
Defining roles + sharing the Dashboard.
Read or act?
Act: create and edit roles.
Who
Admin only
Pairs with
The Users screen, which assigns roles.

Finding it

Click Admin at the bottom of the icon rail (it opens on this screen), and use the sidebar to move between Roles & permissions, Users and Spaces. Admin does not appear for anyone who is not an admin.

What a role is built from

A Docket role is a name plus up to four switches. The first two control the task manager; the last two control the Plan:

SwitchWhat it grants
See all org tasks + the review dashboardOrg-wide read access and the Dashboard. This is the Reviewer.
Manage roles, assign users & edit/abandon any taskFull management on top. This is the Admin.
Super admin: the plan register: themes, milestones, targetsThe Founder. Full control of the Plan, including targets and founders-only themes. It also turns on the Admin switch.
Founders’ Associate: review packs + the plan register (never targets or restricted themes)The Associate. Read-only access to the plan register and the review for any team.

A role with neither switch on is the baseline Member, a real, useful tier (own + team + collaborator tasks), not a locked-out account.

⚠ Admin always includes “see all”

You cannot give someone the management switch without the see-all switch, the screen turns it on for you and won't let you turn it off. It makes no sense to manage tasks you can't see, so Docket guards against it.

⚠ Only a Founder can touch the two Plan switches

A role that carries Super admin or Founders’ Associate is locked for everyone but a Founder: only a Founder can create, edit or delete one, and the two switches are dimmed with only a super admin can grant this for everyone else. The super admin switch always turns Admin on, as Admin turns see-all on.

Working with roles

  1. Review the role cards. Each shows its name, what it grants, and whether it is a built-in system role.
  2. New Role creates a custom one: give it a key, a label, an optional description, and flip the switches.
  3. Edit adjusts a role. For a system role you can change only its label and description, its switches are fixed.
  4. Delete removes a custom role. You cannot delete a system role, nor one that still has people assigned to it.
ⓘ The three built-in roles

Docket ships with three system roles: Admin (both switches), Employee (no switches, the baseline), and Reviewer (see-all only). For most companies these are all you need; custom roles are there if you want to name access differently for your own teams.

Dashboard sharing

Like every admin screen, this one is laid out as cards. At the top is a Dashboard sharing card, above the Roles card. It controls who can open the founder Dashboard, separately from any role, so you can give someone the company overview without giving them access to everything. Two controls:

Visible to everyone

A single toggle. When on, every employee, present and future, can open the Dashboard.

Specific people

Grant the Dashboard to named individuals. Only people with a Docket login can be added. When “visible to everyone” is on, this list is dimmed but kept, so flipping the toggle off restores exactly the grants you had.

✓ Sharing the view, not the tasks

People you grant the Dashboard to see the org-wide numbers, but clicking through still shows only their own tasks. It is a safe way to give leads and stakeholders the high-level picture without exposing every task in the company.

chapters.title: Users
chapters.html:
The Users screen is where an admin gives each person their Docket role. It is a simple list of everyone at LOT with a dropdown next to each name, that is the whole job.

What it’s for
Assigning a role to each person.
Read or act?
Act: set one role per person.
Who
Admin only
Pairs with
Roles & Permissions, which defines the roles.

Finding it

Click Admin at the bottom of the icon rail, then Users in the sidebar. The page is a single card with a search box in its header.

Reading the list

Each row is one LOT user: their name, email, and current Docket role. Someone with no role shows as baseline (default), which is the full Member tier, not a problem to fix. Search the list by name or email using the box in the header.

Assigning a role

  1. Find the person by scrolling or searching.
  2. Open the dropdown in their Assign column.
  3. Choose a role, or — none (baseline) — to return them to the Member default. It saves immediately.
ⓘ Accounts come from elsewhere

This screen does not create or remove people, accounts are managed centrally. The Users list shows everyone who can sign in; here you only set their task-manager access. If someone is missing from the list, their account hasn't been set up yet.

ⓘ Plan roles are a Founder’s to give

Roles that carry the Founder (super admin) or Founders’ Associate switch appear greyed out in the dropdown unless you are a Founder, and the dropdown of a person who already holds one is locked. Ask a Founder to assign or change those.

⚠ Most people need no role

The baseline Member tier already lets people create tasks and see their own and their team's work. Only assign Reviewer or Admin to those who genuinely need to see across the whole company or manage access. When in doubt, leave someone on baseline.

chapters.title: Spaces (Admin)
chapters.html:
The admin Spaces screen lists every space in Docket so admins can keep an eye on the registry, and step into an orphaned private space when its owner is gone. It is the one and only sanctioned way an admin can enter a private space.

What it’s for
Overseeing spaces; rescuing orphaned ones.
Read or act?
Read, plus the audited recover action.
Who
Admin only
Shows
Space names & counts, never their tasks.

Finding it

Click Admin at the bottom of the icon rail, then Spaces in the sidebar. The sidebar lists the three admin pages (Roles & permissions, Users, Spaces), and the page is a card containing the table below.

What you can and cannot see

⛔ Metadata only, never contents

This screen shows each space's name, visibility, owner, member count and creation date, and nothing more. As an admin you can see that a private space exists and who owns it, but you cannot read a single task inside it from here. The wall holds even on the admin screen.

Reading the table

ColumnShows
SpaceIts name, with a hash icon for General (open) or a padlock for a private space. Archived spaces are dimmed and marked.
Visibility“Open” (General) or “Private”.
OwnerWho owns the private space (General has no owner).
MembersHow many people are in it.
CreatedWhen it was made.
ⓘ The Founders’ space

One space is special: the Founders’ space, which holds tasks linked to founders-only plan items. Only Founders can be members. It has no Recover button, it cannot be archived, and moving a task out of it needs a Founder.

Break-glass recovery

If a private space is orphaned, its owner has left and no remaining member can manage it, an admin can recover it. The Recover button on a private space makes you its owner and a member, so the space can be managed again.

⚠ Recovery is a deliberate, logged act

Recovering a space is “breaking glass”: it is meant for genuine emergencies, not casual snooping. The action asks you to confirm, and it is permanently recorded in that space's audit trail. Use it only when there is no owner left to do the right thing, the everyday answer is for an owner to transfer ownership before they leave.

ⓘ After recovery

Once you recover a space you become its owner, so you can then re-assign it: add the right people as members and transfer ownership to whoever should run it. Recovery is a means to hand the space back, not to take it over.
